topic: After notes on simplifying a proof (using a definite-integral formula or Schlömilch's Compendium), Hilbert formulates every mathematical problem as deciding, by finitely many operations, whether a rule-generated 0-1 sequence ever contains a 0, and claims that every mathematical problem is solvable.

triage.modern_statement: Is there an n such that the decimal digits of π in positions n, n+1, …, n+9 (after the decimal point) are all 7? In other words, does the string 7777777777 occur in π's decimal expansion? Hilbert used this as an example of a problem decided by checking a rule-generated sequence. His 'etc.' points to the general question of whether every finite digit string occurs in π, which is closely tied to the open question of whether π is normal.
triage.answered_by: Yasumasa Kanada (with Takahashi), University of Tokyo, in 1997. Their record computation of π to about 51.5 billion digits found a run of ten consecutive 7s. Richard Zach gives its starting position as digit 22,869,046,249. The question was settled by computing digits, not by a general proof. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is, however, well known as the kind of counterexample Brouwer and Heyting used in intuitionism (their best-known versions ask about '0123456789' or long runs of 7s in π), and Penrose cited it again in 1989.

evidence.claim: Bailey, Borwein et al. (AMS Notices, 2013) say Penrose, in the 1989 first edition of The Emperor's New Mind, declared that humankind likely will never know whether π contains ten consecutive 7s. They add that Kanada found the string in 1997, and that Penrose's second edition changed the example to twenty consecutive 7s.
The same passage, in a version on David H. Bailey's site, connects the question to Brouwer and Heyting's intuitionist examples of undecided hypotheses about π's digits.
Richard Zach notes that Brouwer's and Heyting's example '0123456789' first occurs at digit 17,387,594,880. He also notes that ten consecutive 7s start at digit 22,869,046,249.
Kanada and Takahashi computed 51,539,600,000 digits of π in July 1997.
Brouwer used the question of whether '0123456789' occurs in π's decimal expansion as his example of an assertion that could not yet be decided.
OEIS A096761 lists the position where exactly n consecutive 7s first occur in π.
MathWorld says it is not known whether π is normal. That is the general question behind the 'etc.', and it remains open.

triage.why: The specific question about ten 7s was answered 'yes' by computation in 1997 (Kanada), as several sources confirm, so it is no longer a research question. Hilbert's 'etc.' gestures at the general family of questions: does an arbitrary digit pattern, or an arbitrarily long run, occur in π? For any particular finite string, more computing can only confirm that it occurs; it can never show that it is absent. Questions about all strings at once reduce to the normality of π. That is still open and studied in the theory of normal numbers, but this specific item is closed. I could not find a source discussing Hilbert's own diary note, so the link to Brouwer and Penrose is through the shared example, not through any documented influence.
